extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne; students of philosophy and literature; general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading/analysis of Montaigne's essays (sections on wealth, reputation, and inequality) presenting normative claims about how to value goods, judge men, and live. The text mixes personal anecdote, philosophical maxims, and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value is conferred by opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Our opinion gives the value to things: we often prize things not for their use but for what we or their price add to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'That our opinion gives the value to things is very manifest... we only repute for value in them, not what they bring to us, but what we add to them.' Examples and metaphors: 'the price gives value to the diamond; difficulty to virtue; suffering to devotion; and griping to physic.' Anecdote of a person throwing crowns into the sea to be 'poor.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth does not remove anxiety; abundance breeds avarice
rubrics_metrics.description: To be rich is not necessarily relief; abundance often creates more anxiety, care, and avarice than want does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements: 'to be rich is no relief, but only an alteration, of affairs... In truth, it is not want, but rather abundance, that creates avarice.' Detailed personal examples: hoarding led to fear of roads, distrust of baggage-carriers, anxiety over leaving a cash-box; 'there is more trouble in keeping money than in getting it.' Quote: 'Fortuna vitrea est: tum, quum splendet, frangitur.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Live at the height of your revenue (moderation in saving/spending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a balanced third way: live within current means, saving only for contemplated purposes (pleasures) rather than accumulating reserves that produce fear and avarice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne's three life-conditions: dependence on others, hoarding, then living 'at the height of my revenue' — 'I live from hand to mouth... I content myself in having sufficient for my present and ordinary expense; for as to extraordinary occasions, all the laying up in the world would never suffice.' Illustrative story: Dionysius returning treasure because the man learned to use it; citation of Cicero and proverbs supporting moderate saving for use rather than endless accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pursue reputation at the expense of substantial goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit of fame and reputation is a vain humour that leads people to abandon real goods (health, peace, riches, life) for an empty phantom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim: 'Of all the follies of the world, that which is most universally received is the solicitude of reputation and glory...' Example observations: philosophers too often desire their names known; even critics wish their books to appear under their names. Quotation from Tasso and Cicero to emphasize the vanity and emptiness of fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not communicate one's honour (don't vest others with your glory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's honour is rarely shared; to 'communicate' or give another the better part of one's honour is unusual and often involves admirable self-abnegation or deliberate strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes this as a distinct social norm: 'All other things are communicable and fall into commerce: we lend our goods and stake our lives... but to communicate a man's honour... is very rarely seen.' Examples: Catulus Luctatius feigning cowardice to save troops' honour; Antonio de Leva opposing an expedition so the glory would be attributed to his master; King Edward refusing to steal his son's honour in battle; Laelius supporting Scipio's renown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge men by intrinsic qualities, not external trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess a person by their inner qualities—soul, courage, self-sufficiency—rather than by external marks such as wealth, titles, clothes, or possessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit injunction: 'Measure him without his stilts; let him lay aside his revenues and his titles; let him present himself in his shirt. Then examine... What soul has he? Is she beautiful, capable, and happily provided of all her faculties?' Comparisons: inspecting a horse stripped of trappings to judge its true quality; Latin and classical citations (Seneca, Horace) reinforce the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruition, not possession, renders goods valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing goods is insufficient; the owner must be able to enjoy and use them—fruition, not mere possession, makes them good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: '‘Tis fruition, and not possession, that renders us happy.' Examples: a gouty or ailing man cannot enjoy wealth; a blind man cannot relish pictures; Plato's remark that goods are equally evil to the unjust and good to the just—utility depends on the user's capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur and abundance reduce pleasure through satiety and conspicuousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess and conspicuous wealth dull pleasures (satiety) and create unease because great people become overly conspicuous and lose simple delights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: 'Nothing is so distasteful and clogging as abundance... the relish of them grows flat and insipid.' Examples: singing-boys who tire of music; princes disguising themselves to enjoy humble life; the grand signor overwhelmed by numbers in his seraglio; many attendants (e.g., thousands of falconers) diminishing the pleasure of the sport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on fortune; accept uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune is changeable and unreliable (like glass); one should not expect to be fully armed against fortune by hoarding—uncertainty is inherent and widespread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxim: 'Fortune is glass: in its greatest brightness it breaks.' Examples: people depending on princes, merchants who sell farms to begin trade, Caesar running into debt to gain power. Montaigne emphasizes that most of the world lives under uncertainty and that putting absolute trust in outward certainties is mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence in another's virtue reflects one's own and can enable delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: Trusting others with one's affairs demonstrates personal virtue and may free one from the burdens of management—God favors such confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an aged prelate who stripped himself of purse and revenues, entrusting servants and living quietly; 'The confidence in another man's virtue is no light evidence of a man's own.' Montaigne praises regulated delegation that yields a well-governed household without constant care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is self-governance and indifference to external goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal (wise) person is self-governed: not terrified by poverty, death, or chains; able to resist appetites and contemn honours; self-contained and master of his own fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted ideal: 'Sapiens, sibique imperiosus... Quern neque pauperies, neque mors, neque vincula terrent...' Montaigne contrasts such a figure with common people and elevates internal mastery over external rank: 'such a man is five hundred cubits above kingdoms and duchies.' Classical citations support the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Our perception of pain/pleasure depends on constitution; choose proportionate remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Things (study, abstinence, frugality, exercise) are not painful in themselves but seem so because of our weakness or constitution; one should pick remedies adapted to one's own temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: 'Study is a torment to an idle man... the things are not so painful and difficult of themselves, but our weakness or cowardice makes them so.' Advice: if one cannot adopt strong remedies (philosophical fortitude) one may at least take lenitives to ease the burden. Cited Cicero passage about commending oneself.
